newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zedillo aims for growth with new Mexican econ pact.
newsitem.headline: Zedillo aims for growth with new Mexican econ pact.

text.p: The Mexican government signed a new economic pact for 1997 with business and labor on Saturday, saying recovery from recession was now well under way and pledging faster growth in the future.
"Recovery is now reaching clearly into all spheres of production," President Ernesto Zedillo said in a speech after the signing ceremony at his official residence of Los Pinos.
The new pact "allows us to propose for 1997 a definitive step toward the growth that Mexico needs."

The accord, officially called the Alliance for Growth, set a target of at least three percent Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth this year, rising to at least four percent next year and five to six percent annually thereafter.
It also predicted inflation, which skyrocketed after the December 1994 peso crash, would be reined back to 15 percent in 1997 from more than 50 percent last year and about half that rate this year.

The pact, final details of which were thrashed out in an all-night meeting that ended about 5 a.m. (1000 GMT) on Saturday, set an increase in the minimum wage of 17 percent, effective from Dec. 1 and valid for all of next year.
Absent from the signing ceremony was veteran labor boss Fidel Velazquez, who at the age of 96 still heads the powerful Confederation of Mexican Workers.
Velazquez is recovering from a recent bout of pneumonia.
It also set price increases in gasoline of eight percent from December and 1.03 percent a month thereafter and maintained a 1.2 percent monthly increase in residential electricity rates.
The current floating exchange rate regime for the peso, brought in after the peso crash, would be maintained.
Mexico would run a small budget deficit of 0.5 percent of GDP in 1997 and a current account deficit of less than two percent of GDP.
Business leaders won several tax incentives for higher investment and employment in return for their acceptance of minimum wage increases higher than inflation.
Mexican public investment would be equivalent to 3.5 percent of GDP in 1997, with big increases in real terms for oil exploration and production and electricity generation.
Zedillo nevertheless said that maintaining fiscal discipline would be a top priority for his government.

The tripartite accord, which changes its official name every year but is universally known as the Pacto, was established in 1987 by then-president Miguel de la Madrid as a tool to control inflation and foster growth, and has been renewed every year since.
